steps: Identify what you need to find: magnification, image size, or actual size
Check units — convert both sizes to the same unit before calculating
Use ×1000 going smaller (mm→μm→nm) or ÷1000 going larger (nm→μm→mm)
Substitute into the magnification equation and calculate
State your answer with the correct unit (magnification has no unit)
method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
Magnification questions always involve three quantities — magnification, image size and actual size. You'll be given two and asked to find the third.

Approach:

  1. Identify which quantity you need to find
  2. Check the units — both sizes must be in the same unit before you divide
  3. Convert if needed: multiply by 1000 going smaller (mm → μm → nm), divide by 1000 going larger
  4. Substitute and calculate
  5. If asked for actual size, rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to convert units before dividing — if image is in mm and real size is in μm, convert one first
  • Dividing the wrong way round — magnification = image ÷ actual, NOT actual ÷ image
  • Leaving magnification with a unit — magnification has no unit
  • Standard form errors — count your zeros carefully for very small cell sizes

exam_context.frequency: Very common — appears regularly and links to Required Practical 1 (microscopy)

gold.display: A ribosome has a diameter of 25 nm. Express this in metres, giving your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. So 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. Adjust to correct standard form.
nm to m: 25 nm = 25 × 10⁻⁹ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. Don't confuse nm (10⁻⁹) with μm (10⁻⁶).

gold.display: An electron micrograph shows a mitochondrion at ×40,000 magnification. The image is 80 mm long. Calculate the actual length in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 80 mm = 80,000 μm. Then 80,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2 μm.
You must convert mm to μm before dividing: 80 mm = 80,000 μm. 80,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2 μm.

gold.display: A white blood cell has an actual diameter of 12 μm. A red blood cell has an actual diameter of 7 μm. How many times wider is the white blood cell than the red blood cell? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: Divide the larger by the smaller: 12 ÷ 7 = 1.714… ≈ 1.7 times wider.
The question asks how many times wider, so divide (12 ÷ 7 ≈ 1.7), don't subtract (12 − 7 = 5).

gold.display: A student measures an image of a cell as 45 mm. The actual cell is 0.015 mm. Calculate the magnification, then determine if this cell is likely to be a bacterium (1–5 μm), an animal cell (10–30 μm), or a plant cell (10–100 μm).

misconceptions.message: Magnification = 45 ÷ 0.015 = 3000. Actual size = 0.015 mm = 15 μm. This fits 10–30 μm = animal cell.
0.015 mm = 15 μm (multiply by 1000). 15 μm fits the range of an animal cell (10–30 μm).

gold.display: A virus is 300 nm in diameter. An electron microscope produces an image 18 mm across. Calculate the magnification.

misconceptions.message: Convert image: 18 mm = 18,000 μm = 18,000,000 nm. Magnification = 18,000,000 ÷ 300 = ×60,000.

gold.display: A student measures the image of a bacterial cell as 14 mm under ×4000 magnification. Another student measures the image of a plant cell as 48 mm under ×800 magnification. Which cell has the larger actual size, and by how many μm?

misconceptions.message: Bacterium: 14 mm = 14,000 μm, actual = 14,000 ÷ 4000 = 3.5 μm. Plant: 48 mm = 48,000 μm, actual = 48,000 ÷ 800 = 60 μm. Difference = 60 − 3.5 = 56.5 μm.
Don't compare image sizes — compare actual sizes. A larger image doesn't mean a larger cell if the magnification is higher.

bronze.display: A plant cell has an actual size of 100 μm. Under a microscope the image is 40 mm long. Calculate the magnification. (Convert the image to μm first.)

misconceptions.message: Convert the image to μm first: 40 mm = 40,000 μm. Then 40,000 ÷ 100 = ×400.
Magnification = image ÷ actual, not actual ÷ image. 40,000 ÷ 100 = 400.
Going from mm to μm means going smaller, so multiply by 1000. 0.5 × 1000 = 500 μm.

bronze.display: A cheek cell is 60 μm across. An image of it is 12 mm across. What is the magnification?

misconceptions.message: Convert image to μm: 12 mm = 12,000 μm. Magnification = 12,000 ÷ 60 = ×200.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 12,000 ÷ 60 = 200, not 60 ÷ 12,000.
Going from μm to mm means going larger, so divide by 1000. 7500 ÷ 1000 = 7.5 mm.

bronze.display: A microscope has a magnification of ×400. The image of a cell is 20 mm long. What is the actual size of the cell in μm?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 20 mm = 20,000 μm. Then 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50 μm.
Convert the image to μm before dividing: 20 mm = 20,000 μm. 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50 μm.
Going from μm to nm means going smaller, so multiply by 1000. 3 × 1000 = 3000 nm.

bronze.display: An onion cell has an actual width of 80 μm. A student draws it 24 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 24 mm = 24,000 μm. Magnification = 24,000 ÷ 80 = ×300.

bronze.display: Which of these is the correct unit conversion?

misconceptions.message: 1 mm = 1000 μm. Think: milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶, so there are 10³ = 1000 μm in 1 mm.

silver.display: A bacterium has an actual length of 2 μm. A photograph shows it as 15 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 15 mm = 15,000 μm. Magnification = 15,000 ÷ 2 = ×7500.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 15,000 ÷ 2 = 7500. If you got 0.000133, you divided the wrong way.

silver.display: An image of a cell is 36 mm long. The magnification used was ×1200. Calculate the actual size of the cell in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 36 mm = 36,000 μm. Then 36,000 ÷ 1200 = 30 μm.
Convert image to μm first: 36 mm = 36,000 μm. Then 36,000 ÷ 1200 = 30 μm.

silver.display: A red blood cell has a diameter of 7 μm. A student wants to draw it with a magnification of ×2000. How long should the drawing be, in mm?

misconceptions.message: Image = magnification × actual = 2000 × 7 = 14,000 μm = 14 mm.
Image size = 2000 × 7 = 14,000 μm. Convert to mm: 14,000 ÷ 1000 = 14 mm.

silver.display: A micrograph shows a sperm cell head as 8 mm across at ×5000 magnification. Calculate the actual size of the sperm head in μm.

misconceptions.message: Actual = image ÷ magnification. Convert: 8 mm = 8000 μm. Then 8000 ÷ 5000 = 1.6 μm.

silver.display: An E. coli bacterium is 2 μm long. Express this length in metres, giving your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m. So 2 μm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. The exponent is −6, not −3 (that would be mm).

silver.display: A palisade cell is 0.035 mm long. Convert this to μm.

misconceptions.message: mm to μm: multiply by 1000. 0.035 × 1000 = 35 μm.
0.035 × 1000 = 35, not 3.5 or 350. Move the decimal point 3 places right.

worked_examples.question: A cell has an actual size of 50 μm. Under a microscope the image measures 25 mm. Calculate the magnification.
An image of a bacterium is 30 mm long under a magnification of ×10,000. Calculate the actual size of the bacterium in μm.

steps.content: The question asks for the actual size in metres — we just convert the given 2 μm.
